author: Adel Ahmad
title: "There were many times I outplayed Russell, but his teams won because his teams were better" - Wilt Chamberlain on why he felt he was always better than Bill Russell - NewsBreak
text: There was perhaps no rivalry in basketball history more dissected, debated and for the storybooks than the one between Wilt Chamberlain and Bill Russell . It stood at the heart of an entire era, the 1960s, where basketball evolved from a niche sport into a national conversation. But when Chamberlain himself addressed it, he saw it through a different lens. He didn't see a man-to-man contest defined by grudges or personality clashes. What he saw was a team game where he often stood alone and Russell stood with a dynasty. With 11 championships, no one won more than Russell. He was the image of winning. However, Chamberlain didn't believe it necessarily made him a better player than him. "When I was playing, it was not me against Bill Russell, it was my team against the Boston Celtics," The Stilt said back in 1986. "He had a great deal of help. No matter how great you are, it depends on your team. There were many times I outplayed Russell, but his teams won because his teams were better than mine." That statement distills the frustration and reality of Chamberlain's career. He wasn't wrong. On pure numbers, he towered over Russell. He averaged 30.1 points and 22.9 rebounds per game for his career. In 1962 alone, he put up 50.4 points per game, including the infamous 100-point night. Russell, on the other hand, never averaged more than 18.9 points in a season. Yet, in 11 head-to-head playoff matchups, Russell's Celtics triumphed eight times. The wins went to Boston, but the statistics often told a different story. Chamberlain was a force of nature, breaking records that remain untouched. The numbers leaned heavily his way — scoring titles, rebounding records, field goal percentages. But championships eluded him, especially when Russell was on the other side of the court. Related: "Hey, old man, go sit down over there" - When a practice session with Michael Jordan made George Gervin realize his days in the NBA were numbered Chamberlain's journey through the NBA was not that of a man given a fair fight; it was more a story of individual greatness overshadowed by an unmatched team structure. Russell had Red Auerbach on the bench, orchestrating every move with military precision. He had teammates like Bob Cousy, Sam Jones, Tom Heinsohn and John Havlicek, players who would all end up in the Hall of Fame. The Celtics were a machine and Russell was the heartbeat. Chamberlain, meanwhile, often found himself surrounded by talent that was inconsistent or mismatched. His early days with the Philadelphia Warriors gave him little support when stacked against the Celtics' depth. Even his time with the San Francisco Warriors and the Philadelphia 76ers saw him matched with strong, but not always championship-caliber squads, at least until 1967, when the Sixers finally broke through. That 1967 Eastern Conference finals against Boston was perhaps the most revealing moment. Wilt's Sixers dismantled the Celtics in five games, ending their eight-year reign. It was the first and only time Chamberlain's team beat Russell's in the playoffs. That year, the Sixers were loaded with Hal Greer, Chet Walker and Billy Cunningham all on the roster, and Chamberlain led them with a new approach, passing more, scoring less, dominating with efficiency and control. The narrative flipped. For once, Chamberlain had the better team and got the result. Even in his later years with the Los Angeles Lakers, Chamberlain faced similar frustrations. Though he finally captured two championships, one in 1967 with the Sixers and another in 1972 with the Lakers, those titles often felt like overdue rewards for a man who had spent too long doing everything himself. The media of the time, and often history itself, painted Wilt as the Goliath who kept getting outwitted by the cerebral and selfless David that was Bill. But that framing missed the nuance. Chamberlain was the more dominant athlete, the more complete player statistically and arguably the most physically gifted man ever to play the game. Yet, basketball is not decided by stat sheets alone. And Russell got the rings at the end of the day, which mattered.
